The Japanese Karakusa 唐草 (arabesque vine) pattern depicts an endlessly winding, scrolling vine that twists and branches without beginning or end. Its name literally means "Tang grass," a nod to the motif's roots in Tang-dynasty China, from where it traveled to Japan via the Silk Road and was absorbed into the local design vocabulary over a thousand years ago. Because the vine grows and spreads indefinitely, it came to symbolize vitality, prosperity, longevity, and the continuation of family lineage — qualities associated with resilient, ever-expanding plant life. This is why Karakusa was traditionally used to wrap gifts and wedding presents, and famously appears on the green furoshiki (wrapping cloth) associated with good fortune. The unbroken, interlocking spirals also evoke harmony and connection, as no single curl exists in isolation from the whole.
